title: Invariants and signs
subtitle: The textbook facts, as assertions. Weight moves forward under braking, tires push back against the way they are sliding, left mirrors right, and two independently written pieces of code agree about the same corner. A violation here is a bug, and nothing downstream means anything until it is fixed.
findings: Braking moves 1,215 N onto the front axle at 5 m/s² — about 17% more weight on the front tires than at rest. Double the centre-of-gravity height and you double the transfer, which is the whole reason low cars handle better.

The steady-state solver and the step-by-step simulator are separate implementations of the same physics, and they agree to machine precision about the same corner — the equilibrium one solves for is exactly a state in which the other's accelerations vanish.

Cornering slows a car down even with no brakes and no air resistance. At 0.76 g a coasting car loses 0.036 g, because the front tire's grip points along the wheel and the wheel is turned. A real skidpad test holds speed instead — 539 N of throttle here — and that choice changes the measured balance materially. See FINDINGS F17.

With the manufacturing offsets removed, a car with the steering straight stays perfectly straight: zero yaw rate, zero sideways drift, to machine precision. The tire file as shipped would have pulled to one side (FINDINGS F6).

Doubling yaw inertia slows the response from 197 ms to 397 ms — the car resists changing direction. That is the difference between a mid-engine car and a front-engine one, and it is Episode 8's subject.

checks.name: the_skidpad_protocol_changes_the_answer
checks.detail: A steered front tire's grip points partly backwards, so a coasting car in this corner decelerates at -0.036 g with no brakes and no drag. Holding speed instead — which is what a real SAE J266 test does, and what trim_skidpad now defaults to — needs 539 N of drive and produces no longitudinal load transfer at all. That is not a rounding difference: coasting shifts load forward, unloads the rear, and tips the car into terminal oversteer at 86% of its grip, while holding speed keeps it understeering to 99%. See FINDINGS F17. The drive force is 7.3% of the lateral force here, so ignoring its grip cost (combined slip, open item O2) is a small omission — but it is an omission, and it grows near the limit.
checks.group: Do the solver and the simulator agree?

checks.detail: putting 3000 N through the right rear wheel alone produces 2242 N.m of yaw moment — 1.15 rad/s2. This read exactly 0.0 for the whole of Seasons 1-3 (F72), which would have made every torque-vectoring result in Season 4 a silent null.

checks.name: driving_the_right_wheel_turns_the_car_left
checks.detail: right wheel alone gives +2242 N.m, left wheel alone -2242 N.m. Under ISO 8855 a left turn is positive yaw, and pushing the right-hand side of the car forward rotates the nose left. A sign error here would render a plausible picture of a car doing the opposite of what it did (F36).
checks.group: Does asymmetric drive rotate the car?

checks.name: a_symmetric_split_produces_no_yaw

checks.name: the_moment_arm_is_half_the_track
checks.detail: 2242.5 N.m against 3000 N x 1.495 m / 2 = 2242.5 N.m. Closed-form, and it distinguishes the rear track from the front, so using the wrong one would fail.
checks.group: Does asymmetric drive rotate the car?

checks.name: at_part_throttle_a_locking_differential_pushes_wide
checks.detail: at 1000 N of demand in a 9 m/s2 corner, a welded differential produces -2057 N.m — negative, yawing the car OUT of the corner. Neither wheel is saturated, so kinematics decides: the outside wheel travels further, turns faster, and loses torque to the inside. This is the locked-diff push, and it is the outside check on the model (rule 2) — the sign is not ours to choose.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: at_full_throttle_the_same_device_turns_the_car_in
checks.detail: at 6000 N the same differential gives +1585 N.m, the other way. The inside wheel has saturated and is spinning, so it is now the FASTER wheel and torque flows outboard to the one that still grips. Same rule, opposite outcome — a model with a fixed bias direction can only produce one of these two, and F77 was exactly that mistake.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: more_locking_means_more_push
checks.detail: part-throttle yaw moment: open +0, limited-slip -1029, welded -2057 N.m. Ordered, which is what this model can claim (rule 6).
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: an_open_differential_steers_the_car_neither_way
checks.detail: an open differential gives +0.00 N.m at part throttle and +0.00 at full: it feeds both wheels equally and resists no speed difference, so it has no handling effect to have. That is the baseline the other two are measured against.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: an_open_differential_wastes_tractive_force
checks.detail: of 6000 N demanded with the inside wheel down to 1555 N of load, an open differential delivers 3880 N, a limited-slip 4850 N and a welded one 6000 N. The open diff must feed both wheels equally, so it is limited by twice the weaker.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: differential_parameters_are_ASSUMED
checks.detail: The LSD's torque bias ratio (1.5) and locking fraction (0.5) are [ASSUMED]; a real clutch pack's locking varies with torque and with coast versus drive, which this does not model. Rung 2 (rule 15): the mechanism and the ordering, not any particular hardware.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?

checks.name: track_width_is_only_LIKELY
checks.detail: Track width is [LIKELY], not measured. At +/-3% the moment moves 67 N.m either way; every torque-vectoring magnitude claim must be re-run at both bounds with the CONCLUSION intact.
checks.group: Does a locking differential push the car wide?
